abstract: How epigenetic states shape neuronal responses to experience and memory remains poorly understood. Here, using a quantitative, single-event approach, our study identifies a subset of neurons that accumulate H3K9me3 (H3K9me3high neurons) via the methyltransferase Suv39h1, specifically in the dorsal dentate gyrus (dDG) of aged mice. FACS coupled to RNA-seq showed that dDG-H3K9me3high neurons express a transcriptional state that fails to induce plasticity machinery despite engaging memory-stabilization programs. Using our novel NucleuSynapse-Tag approach, we found that H3K9me3 accumulation interferes with neuronal activation and synaptic remodeling in response to behavioral stimulation in aged mice. Further, genetically inhibiting Suv39h1 to lower dDG-H3K9me3high numbers improved memory in aged mice. Together, these findings reveal a region- and cell-type-specific epigenetic mechanism linking impaired neuronal responsiveness to age-related memory decline, providing mechanistic insight into the therapeutic potential of targeting Suv39h1.
